analysis.one_liner: Raises new-car fuel economy standards to 34 mpg and stiffens penalties for automakers that fall short.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise new-car fuel economy standards from 27.5 to 34 miles per gallon by 1996 never left the Senate Commerce Committee and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have gradually raised the corporate average fuel economy (CAFE) standard for new cars from 27.5 miles per gallon to 34 by model year 1996, using technology the bill's own findings said was already available and cost-effective. It also barred carmakers from letting their fleet efficiency slip below recent levels, doubled the fine for missing the standard from $5 to $10 per tenth of a mile per gallon, and doubled the fine again for repeat violators. It directed federal agencies to report on fuel-saving technology and on the accuracy of official fuel economy tests.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who buys or rides in a new car: higher standards mean fewer trips to the gas pump over the life of the vehicle. The bill's findings tied the standards to two broader public interests — cutting dependence on imported oil, which both Presidents Reagan and Bush had called a national security concern, and reducing carbon dioxide emissions from passenger vehicles, which Congress described as increasingly suspected of driving global climate change [S3]. Because the bill cited existing, cost-effective technology, drivers could get these savings without the auto industry redesigning cars around them [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the new-car fuel economy standard in yearly steps from 27.5 mpg (1989-1990) to 34 mpg by model year 1996, which means every new car sold would use meaningfully less gasoline over its lifetime.

Adds an anti-backsliding rule: starting with model year 1991, a carmaker that lets its fleet efficiency fall below the level it achieved in at least one of the two prior years owes a penalty — so companies cannot coast after hitting an early target.

Doubles the civil penalty for missing the standard from $5 to $10 per tenth of a mile per gallon, per vehicle, and lets the Secretary of Transportation double it again for a carmaker with a pattern of violations across three consecutive model years — making noncompliance genuinely expensive rather than a cheap cost of doing business.

The bill's own findings state that Department of Energy and Office of Technology Assessment analyses showed known, cost-effective technologies already in use could deliver substantial fuel economy gains without changing the size, performance, or luxury equipment of new cars — meaning the savings to drivers would come at modest cost.

Requires the Transportation and Energy Departments to report on available and future fuel-saving technology, and requires the EPA to report on the accuracy of its fuel economy testing, so the public numbers on window stickers reflect real-world performance.

analysis.who_pays: Automobile manufacturers bear the direct cost: they would have to improve fleet fuel economy on the schedule set in the bill, pay doubled fines for falling short, and face doubled-again fines as repeat violators [S2] [S3]. Some of those compliance costs would likely be passed on to new-car buyers as higher prices, though the bill's findings argued the needed technology was already cost-effective and usable in existing factories [S3]. Indirectly, companies that sell gasoline would see demand erode as new cars burn less fuel.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would likely show up in new-car prices. Even though the bill's findings cite cost-effective technology, carmakers would still face engineering and production expenses meeting a mandated 34 mpg by 1996, plus doubled fines ($10 per tenth of a mpg per vehicle, doubled again for repeat violators) if they missed the targets [S2] [S3].

The standards are hard-coded in statute rather than left to regulators to adjust. The bill's own findings concede that 'as we learn more about the threat of global warming... these interim CAFE standards may require adjustment' — an acknowledgment that a fixed legislative schedule could prove too strict or too loose as conditions change [S3].

Stricter fleet-wide averages can pressure automakers to steer production toward smaller, lighter vehicles, which some buyers — particularly those who need large vehicles for work or family — could experience as reduced choice or higher prices for the vehicles they prefer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the bill's own terms, the benefits run to a broad public — lower fuel bills for every new-car buyer, reduced oil imports, and lower carbon emissions — while the costs fall on a concentrated industry that the bill's findings said could comply with technology it already owned [S3]. The main honest caveat is that the penalties and statutory schedule were aggressive, and some compliance cost would find its way into car prices; a poorly designed standard could also squeeze vehicle choice. But the design included reports on technology availability and testing accuracy to keep the schedule grounded. As written, the benefits plausibly outweighed the costs — which makes the bill's quiet death in committee the more significant fact.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 1989 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so the bill simply expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum introduced the Automobile Fuel Economy Act of 1989 on May 12, 1989, joined by five cosponsors — three Democrats (Wirth, Bumpers, Conrad) and two Republicans (Heinz, Jeffords) — giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from the start.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
That is the last action in the record. The full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote at any point during the two-year Congress.
When the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automobile manufacturers are better off because the bill died: they avoid the 34 mpg mandate, the doubled fines, and the anti-backsliding rule, and gasoline sellers keep the demand that more efficient cars would have erased. New-car buyers did not get the fuel savings the bill promised.

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on May 12, 1989.

for.name: Sens. Tim Wirth, Dale Bumpers, and Kent Conrad

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 12, 1989, and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Ernest Hollings
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration or a floor vote; it sat untouched after referral until the Congress expired.

against.name: Automobile manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed tighter fuel economy mandates during this era, as automakers regularly did when Congress considered raising CAFE standards.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — Senator Metzenbaum and three Democratic senators plus two Republicans (Heinz and Jeffords) — but the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record of where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would have forced carmakers to raise fleet fuel economy to 34 mpg by 1996, fined them at double the old rate for missing targets, and fined repeat violators double again [S2] [S3]. What costs the industry here — burning less gasoline per mile — is exactly what saves drivers money at the pump, so the industry's interest ran against the public's.

Cars that travel farther on each gallon burn less gasoline, shrinking the market for the oil companies' core product. The bill's findings framed cutting petroleum imports as a national security priority, quoting both Presidents Reagan and Bush [S3].
